framing: A model is a program whose numbers nobody wrote
paragraphs: Everything in this book rests on one strange idea. A language model is a program, and almost none of it was written by a person. Its authors write the shape of a calculation and leave billions of numbers blank. Training fills in those blanks from data.

That idea is much easier to see in a model small enough to hold in your head, so we start with two numbers instead of billions. You run an assistant, and you want to predict how slow a request will be from how much text it retrieves. A straight line can do that.

The straight line is enough to show the whole loop: choose a shape with adjustable numbers, measure how wrong it is, adjust the numbers to be less wrong, and test the result on data it has never seen. Every model in this book is trained by that same loop, including the ones you will serve in Part 6.

Everything here runs in plain Python and NumPy so you can trace each update by hand before moving into PyTorch in the next chapter. If you have ever tuned a timeout by staring at a graph, you have already done most of what this chapter makes precise.
outcomes: Write a model as a fixed shape with adjustable parameters, and say which numbers are learned.
Score a model with mean squared error, compare it with a baseline, and read its residuals.
Train a two-parameter model with repeated small corrections, then grade it on a request it never saw.
question: If a model fits every example you trained it on, what do you actually know about how it will behave tomorrow?
